claims.text: The starting material is a compositionally homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy with minimal nanoscale ordering or precipitation.
Sustained high-temperature exposure induces local atomic segregation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Cyclic mechanical loading induces local atomic segregation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Local segregation triggers nucleation of nanoscale ordered intermetallic precipitates such as Laves or B2 phases.
The nanoscale precipitates preferentially nucleate at dislocation-cell boundaries and incipient grain boundaries.
Laves or B2 precipitates formed under the proposed conditions are brittle.
High configurational entropy suppresses extensive grain coarsening and intergranular precipitation relative to conventional alloys.
Thermal and mechanical stresses allow local composition fluctuations to overcome kinetic barriers and nucleate ordered intermetallic phases in an initially uniform matrix.
Localized nanoscale precipitates act as internal stress concentrators.
Even a low volume fraction of these precipitates reduces the matrix's capacity for plastic deformation.
Stress concentration and reduced plasticity caused by the precipitates promote brittle fracture and degrade toughness.
Aged or cyclically loaded specimens will have lower fracture strain, Charpy impact energy, or fracture toughness than the pristine baseline.
Precipitation may maintain or increase yield strength after aging or cyclic loading.
TEM or atom-probe tomography will reveal nanoscale precipitates at dislocation boundaries after treatment that are absent from the baseline.
The proposed brittle behavior occurs under sustained temperatures of approximately 600–900 °C combined with cyclic loading representative of demanding service.
At lower temperatures or under short-term loading, the alloy retains high toughness.
Absence of both a statistically significant toughness reduction and emergent nanoscale brittle precipitates in treated specimens would falsify the proposed mechanism.
